name: Fanhuasheng (翻花绳)
blurb: Cat's cradle, Chinese style: two kids pass a loop of string back and forth as new shapes
title: What Is Fanhuasheng (翻花绳)? Cat's Cradle in China
description: Fanhuasheng (翻花绳) is the Chinese name for cat's cradle: a string loop passed between two players' fingers, each turning it into a new figure. Origin unknown.
answer: Fanhuasheng (翻花绳, turning the flower string) is the Chinese name for cat's cradle. One player stretches a loop of string into a figure across their fingers; the other pinches and hooks certain strands, takes it over and turns it into a new figure, and the two keep alternating until someone makes a mistake or reaches a figure that cannot be turned again. It was a classic break-time game for Chinese children, and string games like it exist all over the world; where it began is not known.

body: Take a piece of wool or cotton string a little over a metre long and knot the ends into a loop. Then:

ol: The first player loops it over both hands and picks up the strands with the middle fingers to make the opening figure
The second player studies where the strings cross and pinches two crossings with thumbs and forefingers
Pulling out, then going under or over, they lift the whole figure off the first player's hands, and it becomes a new shape
Players keep alternating; dropping the string, tangling it, or reaching a dead-end figure ends the round

body: You can also play alone, making figures such as stars on your own two hands.

Regional names in China include fanxianxi, xianfanhua, fanhuagu, tiaobengbeng, jiegu, da shizi jie, with fansheng or fanhuasheng common in everyday speech. Figures have no fixed names either; children named them by what they looked like, such as noodles for parallel strands or a feeding trough for the sagging middle shape, and names changed from town to town.

The earliest known English mention of cat's cradle is in a book from 1768, and the origin of the name is debated. In Japan the game is ayatori; many Indigenous cultures have their own string figures. Standard two-player figures in English include the cradle, manger, cat's eye and fish in a dish, and one figure can often branch into several different next ones. In the 1970s, record attempts logged more than 21,000 changes in 21 hours and were listed in the Guinness Book of Records.

ul: A length snipped off a ball of knitting wool, knotted, and good for a whole break
The moment a finger slipped and the figure collapsed into a tangle
A go-to indoor game on rainy days
The one classmate who could make a complicated star alone

faq.q: How long should the string be?
faq.a: There is no rule; a loop from a little over a metre of wool or cotton string works for most hands.

Where did cat's cradle come from?
faq.a: No one knows. String figure games are found worldwide and the first English record dates from 1768.
